original_question: Repeat the empirical data studies comparing the critical beta-splitting model with real phylogenetic trees on a substantially larger dataset, and extend those comparisons to additional tree-shape indices beyond the small-scale studies reported in the paper.
target_in_paper: Section 9.2, Comparing with cladogram data, of the current arXiv version; in the July 2024 version of the same paper this appeared explicitly as Open Problem 10: Repeat these data studies on a larger scale and for other indices.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies that the target is an empirical follow-up rather than a new theorem: it is about comparing the critical beta-splitting model with real phylogenetic/cladogram data, doing so on a much larger dataset than the paper's initial small studies, and extending the comparison beyond the originally examined summaries to additional imbalance-related statistics.
missing_details: The relevant model is the discrete-time critical beta-splitting tree DTCS(n), not the continuous-time model CTCS(n).
Critical here means beta = -1, with split law q(m,i) = [m/(2 h_{m-1})] * 1/[i(m-i)] for 1 <= i <= m-1, where h_{m-1} = Σ_{j=1}^{m-1} 1/j.

The paper's existing small-scale empirical comparisons are specifically the split-balance study behind the observation that, among clades of size m, the median size of the smaller daughter clade scales roughly as m^(1/2), and the fringe-distribution study shown in Figure 9.
For the fringe study, the observable is the proportion of leaves lying in clades of a given unlabelled shape, with left/right orientation ignored; Figure 9 reports shapes with 2 through 6 leaves.
The extension to other indices should be kept tied to additional tree-balance/imbalance indices in the paper's sense, not broadened to arbitrary tree statistics.
The comparison should be done at matched leaf counts n by direct simulation of DTCS(n); the paper explicitly says asymptotics are irrelevant for this task.
The data objects are phylogenetic cladograms/rooted binary tree shapes, not an abstract distributional family divorced from the empirical tree setting.
The paper treats DTCS(n) as a zero-parameter benchmark; that benchmarking role is implicit in the empirical question.
The paper does not specify a numerical threshold for larger scale, so a faithful stand-alone formulation should not invent one.
refined_question: For the discrete-time critical beta-splitting model DTCS(n) (beta = -1), in which each clade of size m >= 2 splits into daughter clades of sizes i and m-i with probability q(m,i) = [m/(2 h_{m-1})] * 1/[i(m-i)] and h_{m-1} = Σ_{j=1}^{m-1} 1/j, carry out, by direct simulation at matched leaf counts n, a much larger empirical comparison with rooted phylogenetic cladograms than the paper's initial small-scale studies: specifically, repeat the comparison of (i) split statistics underlying the observation that, among clades of size m, the median size of the smaller daughter clade scales roughly as m^(1/2), and (ii) fringe-distribution statistics given by the proportions of leaves lying in unlabelled clades of each shape (with left/right orientation ignored), as in Figure 9 for clade sizes 2 through 6; then extend the same empirical comparison to additional tree-balance/imbalance indices, in order to test how well this zero-parameter DTCS(n) model matches real phylogenetic tree data.
justification: The draft is aimed at the paper's empirical-comparison discussion, not at its height, consistency, or scaling-limit problems. The nearby context fixes the stochastic model as DTCS(n) with beta = -1 and q(m,i) proportional to 1/[i(m-i)], identifies the original motivating split statistic (median smaller-subclade size about m^(1/2)), records the second small-scale data study through Figure 9's fringe-shape frequencies, and then asks for a larger-scale repeat for other indices. To make the question stand alone and paper-faithful, one therefore has to name DTCS(n), define the beta = -1 split law, specify the two empirical studies being repeated, note that fringe shapes are unlabelled up to left/right symmetry, and keep the extension tied to additional imbalance indices and direct simulation rather than to asymptotic analysis.
